# Diego García Miravete

Diego Leonardo García Miravete is a prominent figure in the history of American football in Mexico, recognized for his transformative impact as a coach, particularly during his long and highly successful tenure leading the Universidad Nacional Autónoma de México (UNAM) team, the Cóndores UNAM , . His career spans multiple decades and includes not only building dominant university programs but also representing Mexico at the highest levels of competition and pioneering the expansion of the sport into new academic institutions , . This report provides a comprehensive overview of his life, detailing his playing career, extensive coaching record, innovative methodologies, championship successes, and his profound influence on the development of American football across the country. The analysis is based exclusively on the provided sources, which document his achievements, his systematic approach to program-building, and his enduring legacy as a foundational architect of the sport in Mexico.

## Early Life and Education

Diego García Miravete's early life and formative years laid the groundwork for his future prominence in Mexican sports. He was born in Mexico City, the capital of Mexico, which positioned him within the heartland of the nation's academic and athletic communities . His educational journey began with secondary school at the prestigious Escuela Nacional Preparatoria 5, an institution known for its rigorous academic standards . He entered this high school at the age of 15, demonstrating an early aptitude for higher-level studies . Following his secondary education, García Miravete pursued a degree in engineering at the National Autonomous University of Mexico (UNAM), one of the most respected universities in the country . His time at UNAM would prove to be central to his identity and career, as it was there that he would both play and later revolutionize the university's American football program .

His involvement in American football began as a player during his university years. He played college football for two different UNAM teams over a span of six seasons. From 1966 to 1969, he was a member of the Pumas Doradas, the initial team representing UNAM in American football . Subsequently, he transferred to the Cóndores UNAM, where he played from 1970 to 1971 and served as the team's captain in his final season . This dual experience as both a player and a leader within the university system provided him with an intimate understanding of the sport's culture, challenges, and potential at the collegiate level in Mexico. His playing career was not limited to the university circuit; he also represented his country internationally, participating in the 1971 Pan American Games . This early exposure to high-level competition contributed to his deep-seated passion for the sport and informed his later coaching philosophy, which emphasized excellence and holistic development . In addition to his athletic pursuits, García Miravete's personal life included marriage in 1968, the same year he had a son, indicating a commitment to family alongside his demanding career in sports . His nickname, "Lapizote," suggests a personal characteristic noted by his peers, while "Flaco" points to his physical stature, which was reportedly tall , . He is also known to be a fan of the Dallas Cowboys, an NFL team, reflecting an interest in the professional version of the game that likely influenced his coaching methods . This blend of academic rigor, athletic leadership, and personal grounding forms the foundation upon which his legendary coaching career was built.

## Coaching Career and Professional Roles

Diego García Miravete's transition from a player to a coach marked the beginning of a transformative era for American football in Mexico. His professional coaching career is extensive and multifaceted, encompassing numerous university teams, national squads, and a role in expanding the sport to new academic frontiers. His journey demonstrates a consistent pattern of taking established programs and elevating them to unprecedented levels of success through a combination of strategic innovation, disciplined execution, and a holistic philosophy of player development. His first documented coaching roles were assistant positions, providing him with foundational experience before he ascended to head coaching duties. He served as an assistant coach for the Cóndores UNAM from 1973 to 1975, a period that likely allowed him to observe and learn from the intricacies of program management from a senior position . After this apprenticeship, he was appointed head coach of the Cóndores UNAM in 1976, a role that would define his career and legacy , .

The pinnacle of his coaching career was his 17-year tenure as the head coach of the Cóndores UNAM, from 1976 to 1993 , . During this time, he led the team to nine national championships, a remarkable achievement that solidified the Cóndores as the dominant force in Mexican university football , , . This sustained success earned his era the official designation of the 'época gloriosa' (glorious era) within UNAM's historical account of the sport . Beyond his work at UNAM, García Miravete demonstrated his ability to adapt and succeed in diverse environments. He gained international experience by coaching the Cardinals Palermo in Italy in 1995 and the Badalona Drags in Spain in the year 2000 , . Domestically, he continued to make significant impacts at other major university programs. He served as head coach for the Auténticos Tigres UANL from 1995 to 1999, the Borregos Salvajes Toluca from 2000 to 2005, the Linces UVM in an assistant capacity from 2007 to 2009, and the Borregos Salvajes Santa Fe from 2010 to 2014 , . His final documented head coaching role was with the ITESM Campus Santa Fe , .

García Miravete's influence extended significantly to the national stage, where he was repeatedly called upon to lead Mexico's best university talent. He served as the head coach of the Mexican All-Stars, a select team that competes in the Aztec Bowl, on four separate occasions: in 1984, 1986, 1990, and 1991 , . Furthermore, he was responsible for assembling and training the Mexico junior national team for the NFL Global Junior Championship, a role he held for three consecutive years from 1997 to 1999 . Even in his later years, his expertise remained in demand. In 2014, he was appointed head coach of the Mexican national university team for the inaugural World University American Football Championship in Uppsala, Sweden, though he ultimately declined the role due to prior commitments , , . His career timeline, spanning from his playing days in 1966 to his later coaching assignments in the 2010s, illustrates a lifelong dedication to the sport and a career defined by service at every level of the Mexican American football ecosystem . This breadth of experience, from assistant roles to international championships, underscores his status as a versatile and respected leader in the field.

## Architect of the 'Época Gloriosa' at UNAM

Diego García Miravete's arrival as head coach of the Cóndores UNAM in 1976 marked a pivotal moment in the history of Mexican university football . Taking over a team that had recently replaced its previous coach due to poor results, García Miravete inherited a program ripe for transformation . Over the next seventeen seasons, he systematically rebuilt the Cóndores from a struggling entity into a dynasty, a period officially designated as the 'época gloriosa' (glorious era) . His success was not merely a product of chance or superior athletes; it was the result of a deliberate and comprehensive overhaul of the program's culture, operations, and strategic direction. He implemented a series of foundational innovations that institutionalized competitive excellence and set a new standard for professionalism within Mexican college sports . One of his earliest and most impactful changes was the introduction of mandatory athletic testing in 1977 . By instituting standardized benchmarks for events like the 40-yard dash, the mile run, and various gym strength tests, he shifted the program towards a data-driven approach to performance evaluation, ensuring that physical readiness became a non-negotiable component of team selection and preparation .

Recognizing the need for external expertise to elevate the team's tactical acumen, García Miravete brought in U.S. coaching staff from the University of Tennessee in 1977 and 1978 . This move was significant as it exposed the Cóndores to advanced American football strategies and methodologies that were not widely disseminated in Mexico at the time, effectively bridging a gap between local practice and global standards . Beyond technical aspects, he focused intensely on the team's culture and cohesion. He abolished internal factions, or 'grillas,' that existed between different semillero (youth developmental) teams, promoting a unified identity and eliminating divisions that could hinder team spirit . To foster unity and resilience regardless of the outcome, he instituted the 'Hustle' post-game circle ritual, a powerful tool for reinforcing team values after both victories and defeats . He also mandated uniformed training attire to instill a sense of professionalism and discipline in daily practices . These seemingly simple changes collectively cultivated a more disciplined, cohesive, and professional environment.

Furthermore, García Miravete's leadership extended to branding and recognition. He collaborated with Jesús 'Pucho' Malanco to design the iconic black helmet with a yellow stripe that became synonymous with the Cóndores UNAM identity, along with a new corporate brand for the team . He also launched formal annual award ceremonies to recognize individual excellence, such as 'Jugador del Año' (Player of the Year), 'Novato del Año' (Rookie of the Year), and 'Mejor Actitud' (Best Attitude), creating a structured system of motivation and public acknowledgment for outstanding performance . This systematic approach to program management was the engine behind his unparalleled success. Under his guidance, the Cóndores achieved nine national championships, tying Roberto 'Tapatío' Méndez's record for the most titles at UNAM , . His championship years were 1978, 1979, 1980, 1983, 1984, 1985, 1986, 1990, and 1991, with the team winning back-to-back titles in 1990 and 1991, a feat that remains the most recent instance of a UNAM team achieving such a streak in American football , , . Perhaps his most remarkable streak was a 32-game consecutive winning run from 1983 to 1986, the longest such unbeaten run for any UNAM team since the 1980s, cementing his era as a benchmark of sustained dominance in the university's athletic history . This period of unparalleled success, built on a foundation of rigorous innovation and disciplined execution, firmly established García Miravete as the single most influential figure in the history of American football at UNAM.

## National Team Leadership and Achievements

Beyond his monumental success at the university level, Diego García Miravete's coaching prowess was consistently recognized by his appointment as the head coach of Mexico's national university American football team. This role placed him at the forefront of the country's efforts to compete against top-tier university programs from around the world, primarily in the Aztec Bowl, a premier event that showcases the best of Mexican college football against international opponents. His tenure as the national team's leader spanned four distinct editions of the tournament, and his record in these high-stakes competitions is a testament to his strategic brilliance and ability to manage pressure. The Aztec Bowl, held annually at the Estadio Olímpico Universitario in Mexico City, is a showcase event that draws large crowds and garners significant media attention, making victory a point of national pride , . García Miravete led the Mexican squad in the Aztec Bowl on four occasions: in 1984, 1986, 1990, and 1991 , .

His record in these tournaments was one of mixed results, yet highlighted by two significant victories that underscored his capacity to guide the team to triumph when it mattered most. In the 1984 Aztec Bowl (XVI edition), held on December 15, García Miravete's team secured a hard-fought 22–15 victory over Tarleton State College , . This win was a crucial moment for the program, validating his coaching methods on the biggest stage in Mexican college football. However, his subsequent attempts were less successful. In the 1986 Aztec Bowl (XVII edition), on December 20, his team suffered a heavy 27–8 loss to Washburn University , . Two years later, in the 1990 Aztec Bowl (XXI edition), on December 12, they again fell short, losing 41–29 to Southern Arkansas University . Despite these setbacks, his leadership culminated in another landmark victory in the 1991 Aztec Bowl (XXII edition) on December 15, where his team defeated the Oklahoma State University Bulldogs 35–28 , . This win was particularly historic, as it marked the last time a team coached by someone from UNAM won the Aztec Bowl until Raúl Rivera's victory in 2024, creating a 33-year gap between UNAM-coached triumphs . This achievement cemented his reputation as a coach capable of not only building dominant domestic programs but also leading Mexico to victory against formidable American competition.

The significance of García Miravete's achievements extends beyond the wins and losses recorded in tournament brackets. His consistent selection as the head coach for the Aztec Bowl for four consecutive years speaks volumes about the trust and respect he commanded within the Mexican American football establishment. It indicates that his methods, developed at UNAM, were considered transferable and effective for preparing a select group of players to compete at an elite international level. His ability to assemble a cohesive and motivated national team from players representing various universities across the country was a critical skill. While some sources provide detailed scores and outcomes for these matches, others offer broader context, noting the attendance figures and halftime entertainment, which highlights the cultural importance of the event itself . Ultimately, his national team record, characterized by two victories and two defeats in four appearances, reflects the challenges of international competition but also celebrates the moments of triumph that defined his career. These experiences added another layer to his legacy, showcasing his versatility as a coach who could excel in both the long-term, systemic development of a university program and the short-term, high-pressure preparation required for a single, decisive tournament.

## Pedagogical Philosophy and Personal Legacy

Diego García Miravete's legacy transcends his impressive record of championships and tournament victories. A deeper analysis of his career reveals a profound pedagogical philosophy centered on the holistic development of student-athletes. He viewed American football not merely as a competitive sport but as a vehicle for formative, integrative, and character-building experiences that prepared young men for life beyond the gridiron . This philosophy prioritized discipline, dedication, responsibility, and personal growth over an obsession with winning alone . He actively intervened in the lives of his players, stepping outside the traditional boundaries of a coach to counsel them through academic, familial, and personal crises . Anecdotal evidence suggests he would negotiate deadline extensions with professors on behalf of struggling students or provide emotional support during times of bereavement or other personal hardships . This interventionist mentorship model transformed him from a mere tactical instructor into a trusted guide and father figure for many of his players, a role he embraced with unwavering commitment .

This holistic approach was reflected in the physical training regimen he oversaw. The testimony of former physical trainer Felipe Cigala, who worked with García Miravete's Cóndores UNAM team, confirms a methodological consistency where all athletes were expected to work equally hard ("En el aspecto físico trabajan igual todos") . This principle of shared struggle and mutual accountability was a cornerstone of his leadership style. His personal demeanor was often described as stern and decisive. One source paints a vivid picture of a man who was nearly two meters tall, with a strong voice and a proud, haughty, and decisive personality, whose speech was habitually terse . This authoritative presence was complemented by a deeply ingrained set of personal values that he sought to instill in his players. He advocated for direct confrontation ('atacarlas de frente'), dignity in both victory and defeat, and a unique balance of humility paired with pride . His emphasis on personal accountability—summed up in the phrase "cada quien tiene sus propios asuntos y uno mismo los tiene que resolver"—encouraged self-reliance and maturity .

These principles were sometimes imparted through unconventional disciplinary methods. One powerful anecdote describes a ritual where he would bind his own son with adhesive tape during team travel, followed by laughter and quiet joy as he removed it while repeating the lesson, "el que se lleva se aguanta" (the one who gets taken away must endure it) . This story encapsulates the duality of his leadership: a stern disciplinarian who used firmness as a means to teach resilience, coupled with a paternal affection that fostered a strong, loyal bond with his players. This complex interplay of authority and mentorship created a unique team dynamic that was resilient, disciplined, and fiercely loyal. The impact of his philosophy is evident in the careers of those he mentored. José Luis Izquierdo, who played under García Miravete at the Cóndores, later became a coach for UNAM's youth program, establishing a direct professional lineage that traces back to the golden era of the team . This continuity demonstrates that García Miravete's influence was not confined to his immediate tenure but rippled through the Mexican American football community for generations. Furthermore, his standing as a revered elder statesman of the sport was formally affirmed in a sworn attestation submitted as part of a visa petition, in which fellow coach Roberto Rodriguez De La Torre credited García Miravete with coaching programs that won nineteen national championships in college football and fourteen in high school football . While this total exceeds the sum of his documented UNAM and national team titles, it serves as a powerful endorsement from a peer, corroborating the immense scale of his impact and the deep respect he commands within the sport's hierarchy . His legacy is therefore twofold: a legacy of institutional success built on data-driven innovation and a legacy of personal mentorship that shaped the character of countless young men.

## Later Career and Enduring Influence

Even after concluding his primary coaching tenures, Diego García Miravete's influence on Mexican American football did not wane; instead, it evolved, focusing on the expansion and modernization of the sport. In 2018, he was appointed as the head coach of the newly established flag football (tochito bandera) program at the Universidad Autónoma de Aguascalientes (UAA) , . This role was groundbreaking, as he was tasked with leading the launch of both the men's Liga Mayor team and the women's tochito bandera program, the latter with the goal of competing in the 2019 Universiada in Querétaro , . At the time of his appointment, he brought with him an estimated 20 years of head coaching experience at UNAM, 18 additional years with top Mexican university teams, and two years of experience coaching championship teams in Europe, making him a uniquely qualified pioneer for this initiative , . His mandate was to create a holistic development program that integrated physical and mental training for all athletes, regardless of their size or weight, signaling a shift towards a more inclusive and scientifically grounded approach to athlete development . The recruitment drive for the new UAA teams drew an impressive response, with 446 student applicants from across the university, highlighting the appeal of his vision and leadership , .

His commitment to UAA continued, and in August 2024, he was named the head coach of the Gallos football program at the university, initiating a five-year plan to build a comprehensive structure that would eventually include teams in flag, juvenile, intermediate, and Liga Mayor categories . This long-term vision demonstrated his strategic thinking and his desire to build sustainable athletic programs from the ground up. His goal included fielding a women's flag team for the 2025 Universiada in Saltillo, a project that required qualification at the regional tournament in Querétaro . This continued involvement in developing new programs underscores his role not just as a builder of champions, but as a catalyst for the sport's growth in regions outside the traditional powerhouses. His work at UAA represents a continuation of his core philosophy: using American football as a tool for holistic development, academic integration, and the creation of a strong, supportive community , .

To conclude, Diego García Miravete's career stands as a testament to transformative leadership in sports. He began as a player at UNAM, gaining firsthand experience of the institution's athletic culture . He then rose to become the architect of the 'época gloriosa' at UNAM, a period of unprecedented dominance for the Cóndores that was built not on luck, but on a systematic infusion of scientific testing, foreign expertise, cultural rituals, and professional standards , . As the head coach of Mexico's national team, he proved his mettle on the international stage, leading the Aztec Bowl team to two memorable victories against American university opponents , . Throughout his career, his pedagogical philosophy extended far beyond X's and O's, shaping the character of his players through a blend of stern discipline and paternal mentorship , . Finally, in his later years, he channeled his vast experience into pioneering the expansion of American football to new universities like UAA, ensuring his influence would continue to shape the sport's future , . His legacy is one of institutionalization, where he took a promising but struggling program and built an empire of excellence, leaving behind a professional lineage of coaches and athletes who carry forward the principles he championed , .

Diego García Miravete implemented a series of foundational innovations that institutionalized competitive excellence within Mexican college sports.
Diego García Miravete implemented a series of foundational innovations that set a new standard for professionalism within Mexican college sports.
One of Diego García Miravete's earliest and most impactful changes was the introduction of mandatory athletic testing in 1977.
Diego García Miravete instituted standardized benchmarks for events like the 40-yard dash, the mile run, and various gym strength tests.
Diego García Miravete shifted the program towards a data-driven approach to performance evaluation.
Diego García Miravete ensured that physical readiness became a non-negotiable component of team selection and preparation.
Recognizing the need for external expertise to elevate the team's tactical acumen, Diego García Miravete brought in U.S. coaching staff from the University of Tennessee in 1977 and 1978.

Bringing in U.S. coaching staff from the University of Tennessee in 1977 and 1978 exposed the Cóndores to advanced American football strategies and methodologies that were not widely disseminated in Mexico at the time.
Bringing in U.S. coaching staff from the University of Tennessee in 1977 and 1978 effectively bridged a gap between local practice and global standards.
Diego García Miravete focused intensely on the team's culture and cohesion.
Diego García Miravete abolished internal factions, or 'grillas,' that existed between different semillero (youth developmental) teams.
Diego García Miravete promoted a unified identity and eliminated divisions that could hinder team spirit.
To foster unity and resilience regardless of the outcome, Diego García Miravete instituted the 'Hustle' post-game circle ritual.
The 'Hustle' post-game circle ritual was a powerful tool for reinforcing team values after both victories and defeats.
Diego García Miravete mandated uniformed training attire to instill a sense of professionalism and discipline in daily practices.
These changes collectively cultivated a more disciplined, cohesive, and professional environment.
Diego García Miravete collaborated with Jesús 'Pucho' Malanco to design the iconic black helmet with a yellow stripe that became synonymous with the Cóndores UNAM identity.
Diego García Miravete collaborated with Jesús 'Pucho' Malanco to design a new corporate brand for the team.

Diego García Miravete launched formal annual award ceremonies to recognize individual excellence, such as 'Jugador del Año' (Player of the Year), 'Novato del Año' (Rookie of the Year), and 'Mejor Actitud' (Best Attitude).
Diego García Miravete created a structured system of motivation and public acknowledgment for outstanding performance.
Diego García Miravete's systematic approach to program management was the engine behind his unparalleled success.
Under Diego García Miravete's guidance, the Cóndores achieved nine national championships.
Diego García Miravete tied Roberto 'Tapatío' Méndez's record for the most titles at UNAM.
Diego García Miravete's championship years were 1978, 1979, 1980, 1983, 1984, 1985, 1986, 1990, and 1991.
The team won back-to-back titles in 1990 and 1991 under Diego García Miravete.
Winning back-to-back titles in 1990 and 1991 remains the most recent instance of a UNAM team achieving such a streak in American football.
Diego García Miravete's most remarkable streak was a 32-game consecutive winning run from 1983 to 1986.
The 32-game consecutive winning run from 1983 to 1986 is the longest such unbeaten run for any UNAM team since the 1980s.
Diego García Miravete's era is a benchmark of sustained dominance in UNAM's athletic history.
The 1976 Championship Season for Cóndores UNAM resulted in a win.
The 1978 Championship Season for Cóndores UNAM resulted in a win.
The 1979 Championship Season for Cóndores UNAM resulted in a win.
The 1980 Championship Season for Cóndores UNAM resulted in a win.
The 1983 Championship Season for Cóndores UNAM resulted in a win.
The 1984 Championship Season for Cóndores UNAM resulted in a win.
The 1985 Championship Season for Cóndores UNAM resulted in a win.
The 1986 Championship Season for Cóndores UNAM resulted in a win.
The 1990 Championship Season for Cóndores UNAM resulted in a win.
The 1991 Championship Season for Cóndores UNAM resulted in a win.
The Aztec Bowl, held annually at the Estadio Olímpico Universitario in Mexico City, is a showcase event that draws large crowds and garners significant media attention.
Victory in the Aztec Bowl is a point of national pride.
Diego García Miravete led the Mexican squad in the Aztec Bowl on four occasions: in 1984, 1986, 1990, and 1991.
In the 1984 Aztec Bowl (XVI edition), held on December 15, Diego García Miravete's team secured a 22–15 victory over Tarleton State College.
The 1984 Aztec Bowl win was a crucial moment for the program, validating Diego García Miravete's coaching methods on the biggest stage in Mexican college football.
In the 1986 Aztec Bowl (XVII edition), on December 20, Diego García Miravete's team suffered a 27–8 loss to Washburn University.
In the 1990 Aztec Bowl (XXI edition), on December 12, Diego García Miravete's team lost 41–29 to Southern Arkansas University.
Diego García Miravete's leadership culminated in another landmark victory in the 1991 Aztec Bowl (XXII edition) on December 15, where his team defeated the Oklahoma State University Bulldogs 35–28.
The 1991 Aztec Bowl win was particularly historic, as it marked the last time a team coached by someone from UNAM won the Aztec Bowl until Raúl Rivera's victory in 2024.
There was a 33-year gap between UNAM-coached triumphs in the Aztec Bowl.

Diego García Miravete's consistent selection as the head coach for the Aztec Bowl for four consecutive years speaks volumes about the trust and respect he commanded within the Mexican American football establishment.
Diego García Miravete's methods, developed at UNAM, were considered transferable and effective for preparing a select group of players to compete at an elite international level.
Diego García Miravete's ability to assemble a cohesive and motivated national team from players representing various universities across the country was a critical skill.
Diego García Miravete's pedagogical philosophy centered on the holistic development of student-athletes.

Diego García Miravete viewed American football not merely as a competitive sport but as a vehicle for formative, integrative, and character-building experiences that prepared young men for life beyond the gridiron.
Diego García Miravete's philosophy prioritized discipline, dedication, responsibility, and personal growth over an obsession with winning alone.
Diego García Miravete actively intervened in the lives of his players, stepping outside the traditional boundaries of a coach to counsel them through academic, familial, and personal crises.
Anecdotal evidence suggests Diego García Miravete would negotiate deadline extensions with professors on behalf of struggling students.
Anecdotal evidence suggests Diego García Miravete would provide emotional support during times of bereavement or other personal hardships.
Diego García Miravete's interventionist mentorship model transformed him from a mere tactical instructor into a trusted guide and father figure for many of his players.
Diego García Miravete embraced his role as a trusted guide and father figure with unwavering commitment.

The testimony of former physical trainer Felipe Cigala confirms a methodological consistency where all athletes were expected to work equally hard ("En el aspecto físico trabajan igual todos") under Diego García Miravete.
The principle of shared struggle and mutual accountability was a cornerstone of Diego García Miravete's leadership style.

One source paints a vivid picture of Diego García Miravete as a man who was nearly two meters tall, with a strong voice and a proud, haughty, and decisive personality, whose speech was habitually terse.
Diego García Miravete advocated for direct confrontation ('atacarlas de frente').
Diego García Miravete advocated for dignity in both victory and defeat.
Diego García Miravete advocated for a unique balance of humility paired with pride.
Diego García Miravete's emphasis on personal accountability—summed up in the phrase "cada quien tiene sus propios asuntos y uno mismo los tiene que resolver"—encouraged self-reliance and maturity.

One anecdote describes Diego García Miravete binding his own son with adhesive tape during team travel, followed by laughter and quiet joy as he removed it while repeating the lesson, "el que se lleva se aguanta" (the one who gets taken away must endure it).
José Luis Izquierdo, who played under Diego García Miravete at the Cóndores, later became a coach for UNAM's youth program.
José Luis Izquierdo's coaching career established a direct professional lineage that traces back to the golden era of the team.
Diego García Miravete's influence was not confined to his immediate tenure but rippled through the Mexican American football community for generations.
Diego García Miravete's standing as a revered elder statesman of the sport was formally affirmed in a sworn attestation submitted as part of a visa petition.
Fellow coach Roberto Rodriguez De La Torre credited Diego García Miravete with coaching programs that won nineteen national championships in college football and fourteen in high school football.
The total of nineteen national championships in college football and fourteen in high school football exceeds the sum of Diego García Miravete's documented UNAM and national team titles.

The statement from Roberto Rodriguez De La Torre serves as a powerful endorsement from a peer, corroborating the immense scale of Diego García Miravete's impact and the deep respect he commands within the sport's hierarchy.
In 2018, Diego García Miravete was appointed as the head coach of the newly established flag football (tochito bandera) program at the Universidad Autónoma de Aguascalientes (UAA).
Diego García Miravete was tasked with leading the launch of both the men's Liga Mayor team and the women's tochito bandera program at UAA.
The women's tochito bandera program at UAA had the goal of competing in the 2019 Universiada in Querétaro.
At the time of his appointment at UAA, Diego García Miravete brought with him an estimated 20 years of head coaching experience at UNAM.
At the time of his appointment at UAA, Diego García Miravete brought with him 18 additional years of experience with top Mexican university teams.
At the time of his appointment at UAA, Diego García Miravete brought with him two years of experience coaching championship teams in Europe.
Diego García Miravete was a uniquely qualified pioneer for the UAA initiative.
Diego García Miravete's mandate at UAA was to create a holistic development program that integrated physical and mental training for all athletes, regardless of their size or weight.
Diego García Miravete's mandate at UAA signaled a shift towards a more inclusive and scientifically grounded approach to athlete development.
The recruitment drive for the new UAA teams drew an impressive response, with 446 student applicants from across the university.
In August 2024, Diego García Miravete was named the head coach of the Gallos football program at UAA.
Diego García Miravete initiated a five-year plan to build a comprehensive structure that would eventually include teams in flag, juvenile, intermediate, and Liga Mayor categories at UAA.
Diego García Miravete's goal included fielding a women's flag team for the 2025 Universiada in Saltillo.
The project to field a women's flag team for the 2025 Universiada in Saltillo required qualification at the regional tournament in Querétaro.
Diego García Miravete began as a player at UNAM, gaining firsthand experience of the institution's athletic culture.
Diego García Miravete rose to become the architect of the 'época gloriosa' at UNAM.
The 'época gloriosa' was a period of unprecedented dominance for the Cóndores.
The 'época gloriosa' was built on a systematic infusion of scientific testing, foreign expertise, cultural rituals, and professional standards.
As the head coach of Mexico's national team, Diego García Miravete proved his mettle on the international stage.
Diego García Miravete led the Aztec Bowl team to two memorable victories against American university opponents.
Throughout his career, Diego García Miravete's pedagogical philosophy extended far beyond X's and O's.
Diego García Miravete's pedagogical philosophy shaped the character of his players through a blend of stern discipline and paternal mentorship.
In his later years, Diego García Miravete channeled his vast experience into pioneering the expansion of American football to new universities like UAA.
Diego García Miravete's influence would continue to shape the sport's future.
Diego García Miravete's legacy is one of institutionalization, where he took a promising but struggling program and built an empire of excellence.
Diego García Miravete left behind a professional lineage of coaches and athletes who carry forward the principles he championed.

**Diego Leonardo García Miravete** is a Mexican former [gridiron football](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gridiron_football "Gridiron football") coach and player. He is considered by many to be one of the greatest Mexican [college football](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/College_football "College football") coaches of all time, and is best known as the [head coach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Head_coach "Head coach") of the [Cóndores UNAM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C%C3%B3ndores_UNAM "Cóndores UNAM") from 1976 to 1993. During his 18-year tenure as the team's head coach, he amassed nine national championships, tying [Roberto "Tapatío" Méndez](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Roberto_%22Tapat%C3%ADo%22_M%C3%A9ndez&action=edit&redlink=1 "Roberto \"Tapatío\" Méndez (page does not exist)") ([es](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roberto_%22Tapat%C3%ADo%22_M%C3%A9ndez "es:Roberto \"Tapatío\" Méndez")) for the most in Mexican history. García Miravete also served as head coach of the [Auténticos Tigres UANL](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aut%C3%A9nticos_Tigres_UANL "Auténticos Tigres UANL"), the [Borregos Salvajes Toluca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Borregos_Salvajes_Toluca "Borregos Salvajes Toluca"), and the [Borregos Salvajes Santa Fe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tecnol%C3%B3gico_de_Monterrey,_Campus_Santa_Fe "Tecnológico de Monterrey, Campus Santa Fe"), as well as stints with the [Cardinals Palermo](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Cardinals_Palermo&action=edit&redlink=1 "Cardinals Palermo (page does not exist)") ([it](https://it.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinals_Palermo "it:Cardinals Palermo")) and [Corsari Palermo](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Corsari_Palermo&action=edit&redlink=1 "Corsari Palermo (page does not exist)") ([it](https://it.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corsari_Palermo "it:Corsari Palermo")) in [Italy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italy "Italy") and the [Badalona Drags](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Badalona_Dracs "Badalona Dracs") in [Spain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spain "Spain"). He coached the Mexico junior national team in international competitions as well. He played college football for the [Pumas UNAM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pumas_CU "Pumas CU") and the Cóndores UNAM from 1966 to 1971, winning three national championships during the height of popularity of the sport in Mexico. García Miravete was inducted into the Mexican Hall of Fame of American Football in 2017. Early life and playing career ----------------------------- \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Diego_Garc%C3%ADa_Miravete&action=edit§ion=1 "Edit section: Early life and playing career")\] Diego Leonardo García Miravete was born in [Mexico City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mexico_City "Mexico City").[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diego_Garc%C3%ADa_Miravete#cite_note-1)[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diego_Garc%C3%ADa_Miravete#cite_note-paternidad-2) He was exposed to football from an early age since his father played the sport as a [guard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guard_/(gridiron_football/) "Guard (gridiron football)").[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diego_Garc%C3%ADa_Miravete#cite_note-God2-3) As a seven-year-old child in 1952, García Miravete was taken by his father to the inauguration of the [Estadio Olímpico Universitario](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estadio_Ol%C3%ADmpico_Universitario "Estadio Olímpico Universitario"), where he witnessed the [Clásico Poli-Universidad](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Cl%C3%A1sico_Poli-Universidad&action=edit&redlink=1 "Clásico Poli-Universidad (page does not exist)") ([es](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cl%C3%A1sico_Poli-Universidad "es:Clásico Poli-Universidad")) rivalry game that sparked his interest in the sport. He attended [Escuela Nacional Preparatoria 5](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Escuela_Nacional_Preparatoria_5&action=edit&redlink=1 "Escuela Nacional Preparatoria 5 (page does not exist)") ([es](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Escuela_Nacional_Preparatoria_5 "es:Escuela Nacional Preparatoria 5")) for high school, where he first played organized football at the age of 15, though he suffered a broken clavicle during his first training session and missed the entire season as a result.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diego_Garc%C3%ADa_Miravete#cite_note-interview-4)[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diego_Garc%C3%ADa_Miravete#cite_note-MA-5) García Miravete grew from 1.68 m (5 ft 6 in) to 1.82 m (6 ft 0 in) ahead of the next season, eventually becoming a starter.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diego_Garc%C3%ADa_Miravete#cite_note-interview-4) He enrolled at the [National Autonomous University of Mexico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Autonomous_University_of_Mexico "National Autonomous University of Mexico") (UNAM) [School of Engineering](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/School_of_Engineering,_UNAM "School of Engineering, UNAM") and joined their team, Escorpiones Rojos, for the _intermedia_ category (20 and under). However, soon afterwards, García Miravete switched to the [School of Accounting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/School_of_Accounting_and_Administration,_UNAM "School of Accounting and Administration, UNAM")'s team, the Gallos, at the suggestion of legendary coach [Manuel Neri Fernández](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Manuel_Neri_Fern%C3%A1ndez&action=edit&redlink=1 "Manuel Neri Fernández (page does not exist)") ([es](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manuel_Neri_Fern%C3%A1ndez "es:Manuel Neri Fernández")), who coached the UNAM Liga Mayor (college) team. By his second year in _intermedia_ in 1966, he was invited to join the [Pumas Doradas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pumas_CU "Pumas CU") in Liga Mayor. García Miravete always wanted to play [quarterback](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quarterback "Quarterback"), but was assigned to be a [defensive end](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Defensive_end "Defensive end").[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diego_Garc%C3%ADa_Miravete#cite_note-interview-4)[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diego_Garc%C3%ADa_Miravete#cite_note-MA-5) García Miravete played [college football](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/College_football "College football") for the Pumas Doradas under Neri from 1966 to 1969 during a "golden age" of football in Mexico where the team enjoyed a national spotlight. "Games were on Saturdays at 4 p.m., the magic hour," he later reminisced. "Tickets would always sell out in just a couple days, and on Saturdays the seats started to be occupied at 10 a.m. ... The sport was an important center of attention." García Miravete helped his team win back-to-back national championships in his first two seasons before the 1968 season was cancelled due to [widespread student protests](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mexican_Movement_of_1968 "Mexican Movement of 1968") and the resulting [Tlatelolco massacre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tlatelolco_massacre "Tlatelolco massacre"). The Pumas had trouble finding opponents to play in 1969 – resorting to an international schedule – and were split into three teams the following year.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diego_Garc%C3%ADa_Miravete#cite_note-interview-4)[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diego_Garc%C3%ADa_Miravete#cite_note-MA-5)[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diego_Garc%C3%ADa_Miravete#cite_note-BR-6) Like many other ex-Pumas, García Miravete followed coach Neri to the newly-created [Cóndores UNAM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C%C3%B3ndores_UNAM "Cóndores UNAM"), where he played his final two seasons. Listed at 1.87 m (6 ft 2 in) and 78 kg (172 lb), he helped the team win the national championship in 1970 and was chosen by his teammates as the [team captain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Team_captain "Team captain") in 1971.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diego_Garc%C3%ADa_Miravete#cite_note-interview-4)[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diego_Garc%C3%ADa_Miravete#cite_note-captain-7) Nevertheless, UNAM football games for all three teams were closely monitored by the government due to the sport's exceptional popularity among students and the university's central role in the protests. Furthermore, García Miravete contends, like many others, that rowdy spectators were planted in stadiums to cause trouble and "make the stadiums unattractive places to spend an afternoon" in an effort to crack down on the student movement. This marked the start of a decline in popularity for college football in Mexico.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diego_Garc%C3%ADa_Miravete#cite_note-BR-6) While in college, García Miravete was selected to represent the Mexican All-Stars in the [Aztec Bowl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aztec_Bowl_/(game/) "Aztec Bowl (game)") against American teams in 1966, 1970, and 1971, with the game being cancelled from 1967 to 1969.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diego_Garc%C3%ADa_Miravete#cite_note-interview-4)[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diego_Garc%C3%ADa_Miravete#cite_note-CDPro-8)[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diego_Garc%C3%ADa_Miravete#cite_note-9) > "The life of the campus was amazing. There were no big movements before, then suddenly everything was happening at UNAM. It was a privilege to be a part of it." –García Miravete on life at UNAM during the [1968 Mexican student movement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mexican_Movement_of_1968 "Mexican Movement of 1968")[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diego_Garc%C3%ADa_Miravete#cite_note-BR-6) > "There's really nowhere to learn coaching American football in Mexico. So, the only real way to learn football is watching their clinics and practices, and taking our film for their coaches to critique." — García Miravete on his motivation to study football under American coaches[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diego_Garc%C3%ADa_Miravete#cite_note-style-10) After his playing career, García Miravete worked two years for [Cuauhtémoc Moctezuma Brewery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cuauht%C3%A9moc_Moctezuma_Brewery "Cuauhtémoc Moctezuma Brewery") before he was asked by his former coach, [Manuel Neri Fernández](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Manuel_Neri_Fern%C3%A1ndez&action=edit&redlink=1 "Manuel Neri Fernández (page does not exist)") ([es](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manuel_Neri_Fern%C3%A1ndez "es:Manuel Neri Fernández")), to return to the Cóndores UNAM in an assistant coaching role in 1973. He was promoted from [defensive line coach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Defensive_line_coach "Defensive line coach") to the head coaching position in 1976 after Neri Fernández accepted a job at the [Universidad Autónoma Metropolitana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universidad_Aut%C3%B3noma_Metropolitana "Universidad Autónoma Metropolitana") (UAM). García Miravete was prepared to resign and follow Neri Fernández to UAM, but was asked by his players to stay and lead the team.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diego_Garc%C3%ADa_Miravete#cite_note-interview-4)[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diego_Garc%C3%ADa_Miravete#cite_note-love-11) As head coach, he revamped the coaching staff, implemented new schemes, updated the logo and uniforms, and instituted team rules to begin building a distinct culture. In his coaching debut, García Miravete guided the Cóndores to a surprise 24–24 tie with the defending national champion [Pieles Rojas de Acción Deportiva](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Pieles_Rojas_de_Acci%C3%B3n_Deportiva&action=edit&redlink=1 "Pieles Rojas de Acción Deportiva (page does not exist)") ([es](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pieles_Rojas_IPN "es:Pieles Rojas IPN")). He also led the combined UNAM selection to a [blowout](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blowout_/(sports/) "Blowout (sports)") win over the combined [Instituto Politécnico Nacional](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Instituto_Polit%C3%A9cnico_Nacional "Instituto Politécnico Nacional") selection in the annual [Clásico Poli-Universidad](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Cl%C3%A1sico_Poli-Universidad&action=edit&redlink=1 "Clásico Poli-Universidad (page does not exist)") ([es](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cl%C3%A1sico_Poli-Universidad "es:Clásico Poli-Universidad")) and was named the [ONEFA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ONEFA "ONEFA") Coach of the Year for the first time.[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diego_Garc%C3%ADa_Miravete#cite_note-12)[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diego_Garc%C3%ADa_Miravete#cite_note-historia-13) In his second season at the helm in 1977, García Miravete decided to contact the [University of Tennessee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Tennessee "University of Tennessee") coaching staff due to the fact that their new head coach, [Johnny Majors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johnny_Majors "Johnny Majors"), had led [Pittsburgh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh_Panthers_football "Pittsburgh Panthers football") to a national title the year before. He got in touch with Tennessee assistant [Joe Avezzano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Avezzano "Joe Avezzano"), who knew some Spanish and invited the Cóndores coaching staff to [Knoxville, Tennessee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Knoxville,_Tennessee "Knoxville, Tennessee"), to observe their spring practices. The UNAM coaches went back to Tennessee the next two springs as well and returned the favor by twice hosting the Tennessee coaches at their own spring practices in [Mexico City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mexico_City "Mexico City"). García Miravete and his coaching staff cultivated such a strong relationship with Avezzano that, when he was hired as the [Oregon State](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oregon_State_Beavers_football "Oregon State Beavers football") head coach in 1980, the Cóndores coaches attended spring training in [Corvallis, Oregon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corvallis,_Oregon "Corvallis, Oregon"), that year instead of making a fourth straight trip to Knoxville. "They came to work," said Avezzano of García Miravete's staff that spring. "They're very organized, very enthusiastic, and a very knowledgeable group of young men. Diego is a hell of a coach, and I'll tell you this: we don't know anything about enthusiasm compared to this team."[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diego_Garc%C3%ADa_Miravete#cite_note-God2-3)[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diego_Garc%C3%ADa_Miravete#cite_note-God1-14)[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diego_Garc%C3%ADa_Miravete#cite_note-little-15) García Miravete went on to visit coaches like [Don James](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_James_/(American_football/) "Don James (American football)") at [Washington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_Huskies_football "Washington Huskies football"), [Jackie Sherrill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Sherrill "Jackie Sherrill") at [Texas A&M](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_A%26M_Aggies_football "Texas A&M Aggies football"), [Gary Barnett](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gary_Barnett "Gary Barnett") at [Colorado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colorado_Buffaloes_football "Colorado Buffaloes football"), [June Jones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/June_Jones "June Jones") at [SMU](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SMU_Mustangs_football "SMU Mustangs football"), and [Lou Holtz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lou_Holtz "Lou Holtz") at [Notre Dame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Notre_Dame_Fighting_Irish_football "Notre Dame Fighting Irish football"),[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diego_Garc%C3%ADa_Miravete#cite_note-16)[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diego_Garc%C3%ADa_Miravete#cite_note-WFAA-17) and credits Avezzano for opening the doors for him.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diego_Garc%C3%ADa_Miravete#cite_note-interview-4) García Miravete led the Cóndores UNAM to nine ONEFA national championships,[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diego_Garc%C3%ADa_Miravete#cite_note-historia-13) building a dynasty known for "their option attack, an aggressive, hard-hitting defense and a deep and talented squad".[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diego_Garc%C3%ADa_Miravete#cite_note-love-11) They won three in a row from 1978 to 1980 and four in a row from 1983 to 1986, followed by back-to-back titles in 1990 and 1991.[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diego_Garc%C3%ADa_Miravete#cite_note-historia-13) In an interview with the _[El Paso Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Paso_Times "El Paso Times")_ in 1987, García Miravete spoke about the keys to the program's success: "sound organization, friendly atmosphere, good image and a winning record... that's what attracts young men to our program."[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diego_Garc%C3%ADa_Miravete#cite_note-19) He opposed player [recruitment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/College_recruiting "College recruiting") and [athletic scholarships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletic_scholarship "Athletic scholarship"), saying that it "would open the door to another type of values."[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diego_Garc%C3%ADa_Miravete#cite_note-style-10) García Miravete and the team developed the mantra "_no puedo dejar de ganar_" (I cannot stop winning). He explained that it meant that they would enjoy championships only on the day of the final and be ready to return to offseason practices the following January with the goal of getting even better.[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diego_Garc%C3%ADa_Miravete#cite_note-20) At the same time, García Miravete encouraged his players to unwind in the lead-up to gameday, such as with team [volleyball](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Volleyball "Volleyball") matches the day before or listening to [rock and roll](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock_and_roll "Rock and roll") in the locker room pre-game. "Players always get uptight just before a game," he said. "One solution I found was that because they are happy, young men, I let them play music, sing and dance."[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diego_Garc%C3%ADa_Miravete#cite_note-21) In 1992, García Miravete was described as "one of the more popular sports figures in Mexico" by the _[Chadron Record](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chadron,_Nebraska#Media "Chadron, Nebraska")_ ahead of a game against [Chadron State](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chadron_State_Eagles_football "Chadron State Eagles football").[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diego_Garc%C3%ADa_Miravete#cite_note-22) After leaving the Cóndores following a poor 1993 season,[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diego_Garc%C3%ADa_Miravete#cite_note-historia-13) García Miravete served as head coach of Italian second-tier team [Cardinals Palermo](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Cardinals_Palermo&action=edit&redlink=1 "Cardinals Palermo (page does not exist)") ([it](https://it.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinals_Palermo "it:Cardinals Palermo")) in 1995, leading them to an appearance in the playoff semifinals.[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diego_Garc%C3%ADa_Miravete#cite_note-23)[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diego_Garc%C3%ADa_Miravete#cite_note-24) He returned to Mexico later that year and took the reins of the [Auténticos Tigres UANL](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aut%C3%A9nticos_Tigres_UANL "Auténticos Tigres UANL") for five seasons from 1995 to 1999,[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diego_Garc%C3%ADa_Miravete#cite_note-25) resigning after compiling an overall record of 17–23.[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diego_Garc%C3%ADa_Miravete#cite_note-26) In 2000, García Miravete served as head coach of the [Badalona Drags](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Badalona_Dracs "Badalona Dracs") in Spain; the team signed eight Mexican players and competed in the [European Football League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Football_League "European Football League") under his direction.[\[27\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diego_Garc%C3%ADa_Miravete#cite_note-27) Later that year, he was hired as head coach of the [Borregos Salvajes Toluca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Borregos_Salvajes_Toluca "Borregos Salvajes Toluca"), who had just won promotion to the top-tier Conferencia de los 10 Grandes. marzo 05, 2014 a las 17:33 GMT-6

![Image 1](http://i.sdpnoticias.com/galerias/2014/03/05/103229_capture20140305103121_medium.png)

Uno de los grandes valores que siempre ha inculcado mi padre donde quiera que ha estado es el sentido de la pertenencia y ésta, de acuerdo a su ideología empieza por la familia; siempre ha hablado de la responsabilidad y obligación de los hijos por corresponder a todo el apoyo que reciben por parte de sus padres; en los hechos ha impulsado el que la familia se involucre con el equipo, con sus hijos, con otras familias, desayunos, convivencias y misas han sido sus herramientas más usuales para dicho propósito, alguna vez hasta una novillada.

Es muy común que en algún momento de nuestras vidas busquemos el apoyo de una imagen, una figura, algo o alguien que represente parte de la identidad que anhelamos hacer propia; es ahí donde muchos pierden el camino, se engañan con figuras, identidades o formas de ser que no son lo que aparentan; todo esto sucede muchas veces aun y cuando en casa tengamos entre otras cosas como principios y valores, una sólida figura paterna; otras ocasiones la madre es quién hace este rol.

En este sentido y haciendo un recorrido muy rápido por mi memoria, creo a mí y a mis hermanos nos tocó compartir con cientos de jugadores nuestra figura paterna.

Tras su salida como coach de los Cóndores y de la propia Universidad Nacional Autónoma de México, su entrañable UNAM, Diego García Miravete se ha dedicado a hacer lo que mejor sabe, enseñar futbol americano, pero el futbol americano que desde su visión debe de ser; formativo, integrador, complementario a la vida académica y familiar, forjador de carácter y herramienta para saber salir adelante en la vida.

Dejar atrás todo lo hecho durante dieciocho años seguro estoy que no es fácil para nadie y para el coach Diego tampoco lo fue, pero salió adelante, siguió su camino y a la fecha sigue dejando huella sin importar si el campo es lodoso, bien cuidado y podado o artificial; con los Cardinals de Palermo, Italia empezó su viaje; en lo deportivo sus números fueron bastante favorables, pero más que ganados y perdidos dejo la semilla del buen futbol americano, abrió una gran ventana de oportunidad para futuros mexicanos, llevó, al igual que con los Dracs de Badalona, España, la filosofía, fundamentos y disciplina, les enseñó que solo con dedicación y esfuerzo se consiguen los triunfos el día del juego y más allá del campo; a lo mejor por esos lados su figura fue siempre la del coach y la del amigo.

Con los Auténticos Tigres de la Universidad Autónoma de Nuevo León la sufrió en serio, uno de los grupos de porras más enérgicos y activos de nuestro deporte son “los Patanes”, como ellos mismos se hacen llamar; pero con trabajo, dedicación y entrega se los ganó, pasó de ser el odiado chilango al coach Diego, en lo deportivo el conseguir los triunfos tan queridos muchas veces toma más tiempo de lo esperado y no siempre la paciencia y la presión aguantan.

Siguieron los Borregos campus Toluca, los Linces de la UVM y actualmente el Campus Santa Fe del ITESM.

En todos lados ha dejado triunfos y derrotas, se ha ganado una que otra enemistad, pero también grandes amigos, jugadores que lo recuerdan con cariño, otros sin tanto cariño pero sí con respeto, con muchos de ellos compartió problemas familiares, económicos, se enteró antes que muchos padres de probables y reales embarazos, fue consuelo ante la pérdida de algún ser querido, le tocó ir a hablar con algunos profesores para conseguir prórrogas para alguna entrega de tarea.

En cada viaje parecía policía de la Gestapo o la Interpol, cuidando el consumo del alcohol, las desveladas, las peleas; muchos creen que no se enteraba pero siempre supo de las paredes rotas en los cuartos de los hoteles y de la obligada redecoración con cuadros para tapar un poco, de los colchones en las albercas y las visitas que entraban por las ventanas; se tenía que enterar de todo para saber hasta dónde podía ser tolerante, otras veces la última noche mejor se llevaba a todo el staff a otro hotel.

Era muy fácil para muchos decirle que los dejara un rato, que no les exigiría tanto y su respuesta era sé que son chavos y tienen que hacer lo que hacen los chavos, pero que lo hagan con responsabilidad, que se acuerden que vienen representando a su escuela, a su familia y muchas veces a su país

Con el paso del tiempo al igual que la relación padre – hijo, la relación madura y con el tiempo aquellos regaños se agradecen o se vuelven anécdotas; muchos de sus jugadores le reconocen el haberles dejado algo bueno en su formación, muchos padres y muchas madres le agradecen el haber sido una buena ayuda, un buen ejemplo cuando parecía que sus hijos perdían el camino, cuando se les salían de control.

Hoy caigo en cuenta que con el tiempo mi padre ha tenido muchos hijos, se los prestaron por un rato, hijos de varios colores, acentos y hasta de diversas nacionalidades, hijos a los que dio y da lo mejor de sí mismo, a todos por igual sin importar si son callados o insolentes, si son primer o segundo equipo, si vienen de cerca o hacen circo maroma y teatro para llegar a entrenar, siempre da y trata de sacar lo mejor de cada uno de ellos no solo para el siguiente juego, o por esta temporada, quiere que den lo mejor para el juego de la vida; y yo digo, si los regaña, los cuida, les exige y los procura como hijos, pues en algún grado no consanguíneo aunque sea putativo han de ser sus hijos ¿no?

Hoy en día ya le está tocando ser coach de los hijos de sus hijos; hace poco Carlos López Sotelo un ex jugador de mi padre compartió esta frase de su hijo; "¡Papá, no exagerabas cuando decías que el Coach Diego es un chingón tenias mucha razón!"

¿Padre y Coach o Coach y Padre? cada uno de los que han sido entrenados por el podrá contestar que ha sido para él.

Es una de las escuadras más importantes del país en el siglo XX debido a que obtuvo diez Campeonatos Nacionales. En 1998, luego de su fusión con los Guerreros Aztecas y las Águilas Reales, el equipo nuevamente pasó a nombrarse **[Pumas CU](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pumas_CU "Pumas CU")**. Durante ese tiempo, los Cóndores de la UNAM fueron la base de las Selecciones de jugadores Pumas que se enfrentarían en el juego denominado "clásico" a la Selección del IPN. La Selección de jugadores PUMAS se efectuaba por el entrenador que mejor posición obtuviera en el campeonato de referencia y era el entrenador en jefe de la Selección Puma Oficial equipo que representaría a la Universidad Nacional Autónoma de México, en el esperado juego denominado "El clásico" siempre contra los seleccionados del IPN. En el caso de los Cóndores, fueron durante su existencia la BASE DE LA SELECCIÓN PUMA, salvo cuando los entrenadores Gilberto Chávez, Antonio Paz y Arturo Alonso al final de Águilas Reales, Guerreros Aztecas y Osos, obtuvieron mejores resultados. Durante los años de su existencia, los Cóndores obtuvieron el mayor número de campeonatos oficiales de la liga ONEFA (ORGANIZACIÓN NACIONAL DE EQUIPOS DE FOOTBALL AMERICANO), siendo los máximos ganadores de campeonatos nacionales del siglo XX de la ONEFA.
